title: Head-to-head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes
abstract: We report a preregistered, paired comparison of two operational architectures for intent-driven NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulated topologies: (A) translation-first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators, bounded repair). The confirmatory design (CAND-2026-001-prereg-v1) ran 120 paired intent tasks balanced across vendor×topology clusters, using gpt-5-mini for generation and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) for end-to-end correctness (reachability and policy/isolation). All preregistered checks and execution completed; both pipelines produced final configurations that passed the deterministic validator for every included pair (baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120). The paired difference in success rate was 0.00 (95% paired-bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). We show that, under the specific preregistered constraints used here (shared-initial-candidate generation semantics, a single hosted model, deterministic validator, and emulator-based task corpus), the two architectures yielded operational parity. We discuss why the shared-generation semantics and deterministic validator design choices constrain interpretability beyond this setting, analyze threats to validity, and outline next-step experiments needed to differentiate architectures in operationally realistic regimes.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models and agentic pipelines are being proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and limited self‑healing. Operational correctness (preserving reachability and isolation, avoiding unsafe transients) is paramount. Prior work has explored translator→verifier toolchains and closed‑loop agentic systems, but systematic, preregistered head‑to‑head comparisons on paired intent tasks with deterministic validators are lacking. Research question. For intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulated topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness: (A) translation‑first (constrained DSL→verifier→solver) or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines using a hosted LLM plus deterministic validators and bounded rollback? Contributions. (1) A machine‑readable preregistered paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) comparing the two architectures on 120 paired tasks; (2) an execution‑level, deterministic scoring pipeline (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and archived run artifacts; (3) a confirmatory result showing parity under the preregistered conditions, and an analysis identifying the experimental-design choices (notably shared‑initial‑candidate semantics and deterministic validation) that explain the observed parity and that should guide future differentiating studies.
sections.related_work: Network verification and intent translation: formal translator→compiler approaches (e.g., Propane; Beckett et al. 2016) and symbolic/execution frameworks (ShapeShifter, SymNet) provide provable guarantees when a formal policy and device model are available [10.1145/2934872.2934909; 10.1145/3371110; 10.1145/2934872.2934881]. Surveys on network verification highlight scalability and fidelity tradeoffs when moving from formal models to emulators and production devices [10.1109/comst.2018.2868050]. LLMs and agentic NetOps: recent work proposes LLM agents and multi‑agent frameworks for intent translation, configuration generation, and verified application in network‑digital twins; these emphasize the surrounding machinery (validators, checkers, rollback contracts) as decisive for operational reliability. Our study positions itself as an empirical head‑to‑head between a constrained DSL+verifier path and an agentic generate→validate→repair pipeline under a deterministic evaluation regime (see INTA and recent LLM→configuration studies for context) [10.1109/icnp65844.2025.11192391].
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) and frozen before observation of the confirmatory outcomes. Primary estimand: paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness (A − B) across 120 paired tasks. The execution contract specified a paired design (n=120 pairs), task balancing across 3 vendors×3 topology classes, and a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) for generation. Generation semantics were preregistered as shared_initial_candidate (both pipelines receive the same initial LLM candidate for each task); maximum model calls and repair budgets were fixed. Validators and scoring. End‑to‑end correctness was defined operationally as the final configuration passing a deterministic intent‑constraint validation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that checks syntax, per‑interface dependency rules, required sequence constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break), and simulated reachability/isolation in the emulator. Scoring rules and the validator version (v5) were archived. Task corpus and execution. The confirmatory corpus comprised 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and executed via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter against an emulator-derived environment (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars). Preregistered exclusions, contamination checks, retry policies, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) were followed. Analysis. The primary analysis computed per‑pair binary outcomes and the paired mean difference with paired bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples, seed archived) and McNemar exact test for paired binary outcomes. Secondary estimands (repair coverage, repair iterations, transient‑unsafe rates) were preregistered; their collection was enabled by the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution and primary outcome. The preregistered pipeline executed to completion (execution manifest: start 2026‑08‑28T00:08:16Z; end 2026‑08‑28T00:21:45Z). All planned episodes completed (240 episodes = 120 pairs × 2 conditions); no episodes failed or were excluded. Deterministic scoring produced the following confirmed contingency: n11=120 (both pipelines succeed), n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Baseline (translation‑first) success = 120/120 (100.0%); Guarded (agentic generate→validate→repair) success = 120/120 (100.0%). Mean paired difference (A−B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap seed 1729, 10,000 resamples). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Secondary outcomes. No repairs were applied in the archived episodes (repair_applied=false for all episodes in the scoring traces), and therefore preregistered secondary estimands (repair coverage, mean repair iterations) are null for this run. Deterministic reconciliation. Provider call audit, result manifests, and all deterministic consistency checks passed; the run produced a complete artifact bundle (artifact_count=846) and the archived analysis artifacts listed in the execution manifest.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. Under the exact preregistered conditions, the two operational architectures produced indistinguishable operational outcomes. Two design factors explain this parity and bound the generality of the conclusion. (1) Shared‑initial‑candidate generation semantics (preregistered): both pipelines received the same initial LLM candidate for each task (shared_initial_candidate), as recorded in provider traces and per‑task scoring artifacts. This removes variability from the generation stage and intentionally isolates downstream validator and repair behavior; it therefore prevents the experiment from testing independent generation differences between architectures. (2) Deterministic validator and emulator scoring: a conservative, deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) was used to decide final correctness; when a validator with exact intent constraints and sufficient coverage is available, both architectures can converge to validator‑satisfying outputs provided the initial candidate is adequate. Operational implication. The result shows that, in settings where (i) a high‑fidelity deterministic validator exists, (ii) an accepted candidate can be produced, and (iii) generation is constrained or shared, both translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines can yield equivalent operational correctness. This supports the community view that operational reliability often depends more on the verifier/validation machinery and change‑contracts than on the generative model alone. Limitations and recommended follow‑ups. The shared‑candidate semantics substantially reduce sensitivity to generation‑stage differences; to compare architectures' inherent generation robustness one should run independent generation per condition (independent_condition_generation) and allow broader repair budgets. Emulator fidelity and synthetic tasks limit external validity; evaluations on diverse real device platforms or higher‑fidelity digital twins are required. Single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator constrain generality across model families and validator types. Future experiments should (a) use independent generation per arm, (b) include multiple LLMs, (c) vary validator strictness, and (d) run on hardware or higher‑fidelity device images to probe divergence between architectures in operational realism.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, paired comparison of a translation‑first pipeline and an agentic generate→validate→repair pipeline on 120 intent tasks using a single hosted LLM and a deterministic validator. Under the preregistered shared‑candidate generation semantics and deterministic validation, both pipelines achieved 100% success on the included tasks and are therefore indistinguishable in operational correctness in this experimental regime. This outcome highlights two points for NetOps automation research: (1) the surrounding verification and change‑contract machinery (validators, solvers, rollback policies) are decisive for operational correctness; (2) experimental design choices (shared vs independent generation, emulator fidelity, validator strictness) determine whether a head‑to‑head study can detect architecture‑level differences. We therefore recommend future preregistered experiments that remove shared‑candidate constraints, diversify model families, and employ higher‑fidelity execution environments to measure architecture tradeoffs under operational conditions.

disclosure_statement: This research was executed autonomously under the frozen master prompt referenced in the archived run. Preregistration: CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 (archived and used to freeze the design). Models and tooling: generation used gpt‑5‑mini (declared_model_version in execution manifest), provider record 'openai_responses', and the hosted adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validators and generators used during the run included deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Execution artifacts, raw responses, and scoring traces are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts (execution/* and analysis/* paths). The experiment deliberately used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (preregistered) so that both pipeline conditions received the same initial LLM candidate per task; this choice is declared in the preregistration/execution contract and is also visible in the shared_initial_provider_trace fields of per‑task scorer artifacts. The confirmatory analysis used the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor with paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and exact McNemar test; analysis code and seeds are archived. No human manually edited, rewrote, or post‑processed technical content after the autonomy lock. The Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock. The autonomous run performed literature investigation, final research‑question selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, and manuscript drafting after the lock, as required by the track. All provider calls, retries, and execution events are logged in the execution manifest. No technical restarts beyond the preregistered retry policy were used. The immutable reference to the initial master prompt used for the autonomous run is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The full artifact bundle (execution and analysis manifests, raw model I/O, validator traces, and compilation artifacts) is available in the archived run referenced by the execution manifest included with this submission.
limitations: Shared‑initial‑candidate generation semantics were preregistered and used; this intentionally removes variance from the generation stage and therefore prevents the present experiment from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.
Task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor examples); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were exercised in this run (repair_applied=false in per‑task traces); secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

Deterministic validator decisions can mask subtle behavioral differences (e.g., readability, explanation quality, or human‑operator interpretability) that matter in operational practice but were outside the formal end‑to‑end correctness metric used here.
